blocks.text: [III, 190] III. The third passage is Es. XIV, 29. (var. XV, 2.): Rejoice not, thou whole Palestine, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken. For out of the serpent's root shall come forth צפע, a basilisk. King Uzziah (under whom Isaiah had been called by God to the prophetic office, [col. 405] Es. I, 1.) had for a time harassed the Philistines with a grievous war, tearing down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod, and building cities in the midst of Philistia, 2 Paral. XXVI, 6. But when he tried to usurp the priestly office, he was removed from the kingship and died in a separate house. He was succeeded by Jotham and Ahaz. Under Ahaz the Philistines recovered their spirit and strength, invaded the towns of the lowland and the south of Judah, and took Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Socho, Timnah and Gimzo with the neighbouring villages, and settled there. For the Lord had brought the Jews low because of the impiety of Ahaz, 2 Par. XXVIII, 18. 19. But in the very year in which Ahaz died (Es. XIV, 28.), Isaiah, full of God, foretells a great reversal of affairs soon to come under Ahaz's successor, Hezekiah, who subdued the Philistines as far as Gaza, 2 Reg. XVIII, 8. Accordingly the holy Prophet says here, Rejoice not, thou whole Palestine, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken; that is: All you Philistines, who once exulted at the deposition and death of King Uzziah, who had punished you severely, and who under Ahaz dared to rise against our people, rejoice no longer. For out of the serpent's root, that is, from the stock of Uzziah, who had stung you like a serpent, comes forth another serpent, namely Hezekiah, and he one of the most dangerous kind, a basilisk, whom to your very great harm you will find more grievous and more hostile than Uzziah himself. Hence Jerome on this passage: Rejoice not, O Philistia, do not insult my people, etc., because the staff that used to strike thee seems broken by death, because the snake has been killed. For in his place will be born a more harmful one, Hezekiah, a regulus, which the Greeks call basilisk, who will kill thee with his look and slay thee with the breath of his mouth. For just as no bird can pass the regulus's gaze unharmed, but, however far off it may be, is swallowed by its mouth, so thou too shalt wholly perish at the sight of King Hezekiah. And he has kept the metaphor beautifully: because he had named a serpent and a regulus, he says that birds are devoured by its mouth and breath. For in Jerome's version the whole verse we are discussing reads thus: For from the root of the snake shall come forth a regulus, and its seed swallowing the bird. The holy man applies these last words to the story of the basilisk, of which Solinus says: It corrupts even the very air, so that no bird flies through the air with impunity, infected as it is by its pestilential breath. And from him Isidore: At its look no flying bird passes unharmed; but, however far off it is, it is burned and devoured by its mouth. And Avicenna: انّ حاني مسكنها طاير سقط [inna ḥānī maskanihā ṭāyir saqaṭa] A bird falls whenever it is opposite its lair. And Alkazuinius: ان طار طاير فوقها سقط عليها [in ṭāra ṭāyir fawqahā saqaṭa ʿalayhā] If a bird flies over it, it falls upon it. So also Damir. But these things are not very certain, nor, as far as I remember, were they reported by anyone before Solinus, who is not the best of authors. [III, 191] And Isaiah is cited for this in vain, since the Hebrew reads, as Jerome himself acknowledges in his Notes, ופריו שרף מעופף, And its fruit a flying serpent (or rather hydrus), which will be explained below. Whoever, then, first rendered those words And its seed swallowing the bird read שואף, which means swallowing, instead of שרף. But in truth there is no need here to search laboriously for reasons why King Hezekiah is compared with a serpent or a basilisk, since it is nothing new for a powerful king to be figured by a serpent. Thus among the Egyptians, who were neighbours of the Philistines, Aelian writes in History, book 6, chapter 38: Τοὺς βασιλεῖς ἐπὶ τῶν διαδημάτων φορεῖν πεποικιλμένας ἀσπίδας, τῆς ἀρχῆς αἰνιττομένους τὸ ἀνίκητον [Tous basileis epi tōn diadēmatōn phorein pepoikilmenas aspidas, tēs archēs ainittomenous to anikēton], that the kings wore painted asps on their diadems, to signify the invincible power of their rule; because, namely, τῶν ὑπ᾽ ἀσπίδος δηχθέντων οὐ μνημονεύεται οὐδεὶς ἐξάντης γεγονέναι τοῦ κακοῦ [tōn hyp᾽ aspidos dēchthentōn ou mnēmoneuetai oudeis exantēs gegonenai tou kakou], of those bitten by an asp no one is ever recorded to have escaped. And Horapollo, book 1, [col. 406] chapter 56: Βασιλέα δὲ κάκισον (read κράτισον) δηλοῦντες, ὄφιν ζωγραφοῦσι κοσμοειδῶς ἐσχηματισμένον, οὗ τὴν οὐρὰν ἐν τῷ στόματι ποιοῦσι· [Basilea de kakison (kratison) dēlountes, ophin zōgraphousi kosmoeidōs eschēmatismenon, hou tēn ouran en tō stomati poiousi] To signify a most powerful king, they paint a serpent with its tail in its mouth in the shape of a circle: namely, to indicate that he rules the whole circle of the earth. Read also chapters 57, 58 and 61, in all of which various virtues or duties of kings are signified by a serpent, whether watchful, coiled, half or whole. But of all kinds of serpents the basilisk is above all the figure of a king. This is signified by the Arabic name ملكة [malika] melecha, the Greek βασιλίσκου [basiliskou], and the Latin REGULUS. Thus Nicander, Theriaca line 397, calls it ἑρπηστῶν βασιλῆα [herpēstōn basilēa], king of reptiles. And Pliny describes it as marked with a white spot on the head, as if distinguished by a kind of diadem. And Solinus: its head lined with white as if with a little mitre. Galen too and Aëtius: θηρίον ἐπὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ τρεῖς ὑπεροχὰς ἔχον [thērion epi tē kephalē treis hyperochas echon], a serpent having three prominences on its head. And Avicenna: مكللة الراس [mukallalat al-rās] with crowned head. And Damir: علي راسه خطوط بيض مثل التاج [ʿalī rāsihi khuṭūṭ bīḍ mithl al-tāj] having white lines on its head like a crown. And Alkazuinius: قال جالينوس انها حية شقرا علي راسها ثلاث قنازع مثل التاج [qāla Jālīnūs innahā ḥayya shaqrā ʿalī rāsihā thalāth qanāziʿ mithl al-tāj] Galen said that it is a reddish snake, and has on its head three crests in the manner of a crown ^{(5)}. They add that it does not, like the others, crawl prone with its whole body, [III, 192] but with its head and the middle part of its body raised. Pliny: It does not propel its body with manifold coils like the other serpents, but advances lofty and erect in its middle. Solinus: When it moves, it crawls with the middle part of its body, while the other half is upright and lofty. As if this were the emblem of kingship, as it was for the kings of the Persians τὴν τιάραν ὀρθὴν ἔχειν [tēn tiaran orthēn echein]. Moreover, every kind of reptile yields to it, however small it is, as though acknowledging it as king; for it puts them to flight with its hiss, as we showed above ^{c)},
